doc.title: Rob Mounsey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 9, 2025

title: Finding room for orchestration, and the sound-expensive era
summary: Mounsey says there is usually room to add parts, and recalls the late 70s-early 80s when producers wanted orchestrations to sound expensive.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It leads me to a question I had. In all your work, have you had instances where people want you to write horn parts or string sweetening and you get a track to listen to and it’s so busy already that you just have to say there’s no room here? Or do you figure out a way to contribute?

That can happen. That can happen. I can’t think of too many occasions where that happened. I mean usually if people want something to be, you know, added to that way there’s usually room somewhere. Sometimes there isn’t a lot of room. You know I lived through a whole era years ago where people wanted orchestrations on everything, say in the late ‘70s, early ‘80s, and big record companies and big producers felt like they just wanted to sound expensive. You know they wanted it to sound like they spent money on it, which is I guess probably not the best reason to be doing that. I’d rather it be done for musical reasons and not just because we want it to sound like we spent money. So there’s
usually a way to add something. Sometimes there isn’t a lot of room and what you add is kind of minimal.
